blocks.body:
Addition and multiplication obey a few laws so basic that they are used without notice: the order of two numbers does not matter, the grouping of three does not matter, adding 0 or multiplying by 1 changes nothing, and an addition can be undone by a subtraction. These are the commutative, associative, identity and inverse properties.

They are what make mental arithmetic legitimate: $4 \times 7 \times 25$ may be computed as $(4 \times 25) \times 7 = 700$ only because the laws allow the rearrangement. Subtraction and division obey neither of the first two laws, and many errors come from assuming they do. Taken as axioms, the same properties define the groups and rings of higher algebra.

blocks.title: Order and grouping
blocks.body: In this page a number means first a whole number $0, 1, 2, \dots$; the same laws are assumed to hold for fractions, decimals and negative numbers. An operation such as $+$ or $\times$ takes two numbers and produces a third. Brackets (American: parentheses) show which operation is done first: $(7 + 8) + 2$ means $15 + 2$, while $7 + (8 + 2)$ means $7 + 10$. Letters $a$, $b$, $c$ stand for arbitrary numbers, so a statement with letters is a claim about every choice of numbers at once. A product of letters is often written without a sign: $ab$ means $a \times b$.

blocks.title: Commutative and associative
blocks.body:
To state a law once for both operations, write $*$ for an operation in general: with $*$ standing for $+$, $3 * 4$ means $3 + 4 = 7$; with $*$ standing for $\times$, it means $3 \times 4 = 12$. The operation $*$ is commutative if $a * b = b * a$ for all $a$ and $b$: the order of the two inputs does not matter. It is associative if $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$ for all $a$, $b$, $c$: in a chain of three, it does not matter which pair is combined first.

The two laws are different. Commutativity moves numbers; associativity keeps them in place and moves only the brackets. In $(7 + 8) + 2 = 7 + (8 + 2)$ the numbers stand in the same order on both sides, so this is associativity alone.

blocks.title: Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative
blocks.body:
For all numbers $a$, $b$, $c$:

$$\begin{aligned} a + b &= b + a, \\ (a + b) + c &= a + (b + c), \\ a \times b &= b \times a, \\ (a \times b) \times c &= a \times (b \times c). \end{aligned}$$

For whole numbers each law says that one collection, counted in two ways, gives one total.

Addition. Put $a$ dots in a row followed by $b$ dots. Counted from the left the total is $a + b$; counted from the right it is $b + a$. For three groups $a$, $b$, $c$ in a row, $(a + b) + c$ counts the first two groups together and then the third, and $a + (b + c)$ counts the last two together and then the first; every dot is counted exactly once either way.

Multiplication. Read $a \times b$ as $a$ rows of $b$ dots. The columns of the same array are $b$ groups of $a$, so the array holds $b \times a$ dots as well (Figure 1). For associativity, put $c$ copies of an array of $a$ rows of $b$ side by side. Copy by copy there are $(a \times b) \times c$ dots; row by row there are $a$ long rows, each of $b \times c$ dots, so $a \times (b \times c)$ (Figure 2).

This proves the laws for whole numbers only. For fractions, decimals and negative numbers they are not proved on this page: they are checked from the definitions of those numbers, or, in the axiomatic description of the [[real-numbers]], taken as the basic laws from which the rest of arithmetic is derived.

Commutativity can be seen in a multiplication table: the entry in row $a$, column $b$ is $ab$ and the entry in row $b$, column $a$ is $ba$, so the table is symmetric about its main diagonal. Of the 100 entries of a 10 by 10 table only 55 are different facts up to order: the 10 squares on the diagonal and 45 pairs off it.

blocks.caption: Figure 1. One array of 15 dots counted two ways: as 3 rows of 5, $3 \times 5$, and as 5 columns of 3, $5 \times 3$.
blocks.alt: Two copies of the same array of black dots, 3 rows by 5 columns. In the left copy each of the 3 rows is circled in blue, labelled 3 rows of 5, 3 times 5 = 15. In the right copy each of the 5 columns is circled with a dashed orange outline, labelled 5 columns of 3, 5 times 3 = 15.

blocks.caption: Figure 2. Two copies of an array of 3 rows of 4, 24 dots in all. Copy by copy: $(3 \times 4) \times 2 = 24$. Long row by long row, each of the 3 long rows holding $4 \times 2 = 8$ dots: $3 \times (4 \times 2) = 24$.
blocks.alt: Two blue-framed arrays of black dots side by side, each 3 rows of 4 and labelled 3 times 4 = 12. Three dashed red boxes each run across one row of both arrays, labelled 3 long rows, each 4 times 2 = 8. Below, in blue, (3 times 4) times 2 = 12 times 2 = 24, and in red, 3 times (4 times 2) = 3 times 8 = 24.

blocks.title: Any order, any grouping
blocks.body: In a sum of any length, or a product of any length, the result depends neither on the order of the terms nor on where the brackets are put. So $a + b + c + d$ and $abcd$ need no brackets, and their terms may be rearranged freely.

Brackets first. Each line below is one use of the associative law:

$$\begin{aligned} ((a + b) + c) + d &= (a + (b + c)) + d \\ &= a + ((b + c) + d) \\ &= a + (b + (c + d)) \\ &= (a + b) + (c + d). \end{aligned}$$

These are all five ways of bracketing four terms, so they agree. In general, call a bracketing of $a_1, \dots, a_n$ right-nested if every bracket is pushed to the right, $a_1 + (a_2 + (\dots + a_n))$. Every bracketing equals the right-nested one, by induction on $n$; for $n \le 2$ there is nothing to prove. A bracketing of $n$ terms is $X + Y$, where $X$ brackets the first $k$ terms and $Y$ the last $n - k$, with $1 \le k < n$. By the induction hypothesis both parts may be taken right-nested. If $k = 1$ the whole is right-nested already. Otherwise $X = a_1 + X'$ with $X'$ a bracketing of $a_2, \dots, a_k$, and the associative law gives $(a_1 + X') + Y = a_1 + (X' + Y)$; here $X' + Y$ has $n - 1$ terms, so by the hypothesis it is right-nested, and so is the whole.

Order next. Two neighbouring terms can be swapped: bracket them together, which associativity allows, and swap them inside the bracket, which commutativity allows. A known fact about orderings is that any rearrangement of a list is a sequence of swaps of neighbours (sorting by repeated neighbour swaps reaches every order), so every order gives the same result. The argument for products is identical.
Compute $4 \times 7 \times 25$ and $36 + 47 + 14$ mentally, naming the law used at each step.
blocks.solution:
$4 \times 7 \times 25 = 4 \times 25 \times 7$ by commutativity (7 and 25 swap), $= (4 \times 25) \times 7$ by associativity, $= 100 \times 7 = 700$.

$36 + 47 + 14 = 36 + 14 + 47 = (36 + 14) + 47 = 50 + 47 = 97$, with the same two laws in the same order. The method is to find pairs with a round sum or product and bring them together; the laws guarantee that the answer does not change.

blocks.body: Compute $14 \times 5$ and $16 \times 25$ mentally.
blocks.solution:
Neither product contains a round pair to bring together, so make one by splitting a factor into a factor pair and regrouping:

$14 \times 5 = (7 \times 2) \times 5 = 7 \times (2 \times 5) = 7 \times 10 = 70$, and $16 \times 25 = (4 \times 4) \times 25 = 4 \times (4 \times 25) = 4 \times 100 = 400$.

Each uses associativity alone; the work is in choosing the split.

blocks.title: Subtraction and division have neither law
Examples do not prove a law
blocks.body: Checking $3 + 5 = 5 + 3$, or a thousand such cases, does not prove $a + b = b + a$: a law with letters is a claim about every number, and only an argument that works for every number, like counting a row from both ends, proves it. One counterexample, on the other hand, disproves a law: $3 - 7 \ne 7 - 3$ settles that subtraction is not commutative. The counterexample must be chosen with care: $a - b = b - a$ holds whenever $a = b$, so testing $5 - 5$ shows nothing.

items.q: Which law justifies $(2 \times 5) \times 7 = 2 \times (5 \times 7)$, and which justifies $(2 \times 5) \times 7 = 7 \times (2 \times 5)$?
items.a: The first keeps the numbers in order and moves the brackets: associativity. The second swaps the two factors $2 \times 5$ and $7$: commutativity, with $2 \times 5$ treated as one number.

items.q: Prove that $4 \times (a \times 25) = a \times 100$ for every number $a$, naming each law. Deduce that multiplying by 25 is the same as multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4, and use this to compute $36 \times 25$.
items.hint: Swap $a$ and 25, then regroup so that $4 \times 25$ is done first.
items.solution: $4 \times (a \times 25) = 4 \times (25 \times a)$ by commutativity, $= (4 \times 25) \times a$ by associativity, $= 100 \times a = a \times 100$ by commutativity. So $a \times 25$ is the number which multiplied by 4 gives $a \times 100$, that is $(a \times 100) \div 4$. Hence $36 \times 25 = 3600 \div 4 = 900$.

items.q: Find all numbers $a$, $b$ with $a - b = b - a$. For which $a$, $b$, $c$ is $(a - b) - c = a - (b - c)$?
items.hint: Remove the brackets: $(a - b) - c = a - b - c$ and $a - (b - c) = a - b + c$.
items.solution: $a - b = b - a$ gives $2a = 2b$, so it holds exactly when $a = b$. Next, $a - b - c = a - b + c$ exactly when $-c = c$, that is $c = 0$, whatever $a$ and $b$ are. For any other $c$ the two sides differ by $2c$.

items.q: List the five ways of bracketing $16 - 8 - 4 - 2$ and evaluate each. How many different values appear, and which one is meant by the unbracketed expression?
items.hint: Use the five bracketings in the proof of the theorem, with $-$ in place of $+$.

items.q: Define $a \circ b = \frac{a + b}{2}$, the average of $a$ and $b$. Is $\circ$ commutative? Is it associative?
items.solution: It is commutative: $\frac{a + b}{2} = \frac{b + a}{2}$ because $a + b = b + a$. It is not associative: $(0 \circ 0) \circ 4 = 0 \circ 4 = 2$, but $0 \circ (0 \circ 4) = 0 \circ 2 = 1$. So an operation can be commutative without being associative.

items.q: Prove that $(ab)c = (ac)b$ for all numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, using only the commutative and associative laws, and name the law used at each step.
items.hint: Regroup, swap the last two factors, regroup back.
items.solution: $(ab)c = a(bc)$ by associativity, $= a(cb)$ by commutativity, $= (ac)b$ by associativity.

blocks.title: Identities and zero
blocks.body: Adding 0 changes nothing, and neither does multiplying by 1. Such numbers are called identities. Zero also plays a second, quite different part in multiplication.

blocks.title: Identity element
blocks.body:
A number $e$ is an identity for an operation $*$ if $a * e = a$ and $e * a = a$ for every $a$. So 0 is the identity for addition, the additive identity, since $a + 0 = 0 + a = a$; and 1 is the identity for multiplication, the multiplicative identity, since $a \times 1 = 1 \times a = a$.

Both conditions matter. Subtraction has $a - 0 = a$ for every $a$, but $0 - a = -a$, which differs from $a$ unless $a = 0$. So 0 does nothing only on the right of a minus sign and is not an identity for subtraction. Likewise $a \div 1 = a$, but $1 \div a$ is not $a$ in general.

blocks.title: Uniqueness of the identity; multiplying and dividing with zero
blocks.body:
1. If $e$ and $f$ are both identities for the same operation $*$, then $e = f$.
2. For every number $a$, $a \times 0 = 0 \times a = 0$.
3. $0 \div b = 0$ for every $b \ne 0$, but $a \div 0$ has no meaning: division by zero is undefined.

1. Work out $e * f$ in two ways. Since $f$ is an identity, $e * f = e$. Since $e$ is an identity, $e * f = f$. So $e = f$. Nothing about numbers was used: the argument holds for any operation.

2. This uses one law not yet stated, the distributive law $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ ([[distributive-property]]). Since $0 + 0 = 0$,
$$a \times 0 = a \times (0 + 0) = a \times 0 + a \times 0.$$
Subtracting $a \times 0$ from both sides gives $0 = a \times 0$, and $0 \times a = a \times 0 = 0$ by commutativity.

3. Division asks a multiplication question: $c \div b$ is the number $x$ with $x \times b = c$. For $0 \div b$ the number $x = 0$ works, by part 2. It is the only one: if $x \times b = 0$, multiplying both sides by the reciprocal $\frac{1}{b}$ (next section) gives $x = x \times (b \times \frac{1}{b}) = (x \times b) \times \frac{1}{b} = 0 \times \frac{1}{b} = 0$. For $a \div 0$ we need $x \times 0 = a$. When $a \ne 0$ no $x$ works, since $x \times 0 = 0$; when $a = 0$ every $x$ works, so no single answer can be chosen. Either way $a \div 0$ is left undefined.

blocks.title: Zero does nothing only in addition
blocks.body: A common slip is $5 \times 0 = 5$, as if 0 did nothing in multiplication too. It is the identity for addition only: $5 + 0 = 5$, but $5 \times 0 = 0$. In multiplication the number that does nothing is 1, and 0 swallows every factor it meets. The related slips $7 \div 0 = 0$ and $0 \div 0 = 1$ are also wrong: neither expression has a value.

items.q: Find $6 \times 3 \times 0 \times 17$ without multiplying out, and justify each step.
items.hint: Move the 0 to the end and group everything else.
items.solution: By commutativity and associativity, $6 \times 3 \times 0 \times 17 = (6 \times 3 \times 17) \times 0$, and a number times 0 is 0. So the product is 0. A product of whole numbers is 0 exactly when one of the factors is 0.

items.q: Does the average $a \circ b = \frac{a + b}{2}$ have an identity? Does $\max(a, b)$, the larger of $a$ and $b$, have one on the whole numbers $0, 1, 2, \dots$?
items.hint: An identity is one number $e$ that works for every $a$.
items.solution: For the average, $\frac{a + e}{2} = a$ forces $e = a$, so the only candidate changes with $a$, and no single $e$ works: there is no identity. For $\max$, $\max(a, 0) = \max(0, a) = a$ for every whole number $a$, so 0 is an identity, and by the theorem it is the only one.

items.q: In the proof that the identity is unique, which of the two conditions in the definition is used in each step?
items.hint: In $e * f = e$, which number is acting as the identity, and on which side of $*$ does it stand?
items.solution: $e * f = e$ uses that $f$ is an identity on the right: $a * f = a$ with $a = e$. $e * f = f$ uses that $e$ is an identity on the left: $e * a = a$ with $a = f$. So the proof needs both halves of the definition, one for each identity.

blocks.title: Inverses
blocks.body: Subtraction undoes addition and division undoes multiplication: adding 5 and then subtracting 5 returns to the start. This is the meaning of the subtraction and division signs, and it leads to the opposite and the reciprocal of a number.

blocks.title: Inverse operations
blocks.body:
The difference $c - b$ is the number that must be added to $b$ to give $c$: $x = c - b$ means $x + b = c$. The quotient $c \div b$, for $b \ne 0$, is the number that must be multiplied by $b$ to give $c$: $x = c \div b$ means $x \times b = c$. So $10 - 8$ is the number with $\square + 8 = 10$, and $32 \div 8$ is the number with $\square \times 8 = 32$.

These definitions assume that exactly one such $x$ exists. Among whole numbers alone it may not ($3 - 7$ has no whole-number answer); once every number has an opposite, the theorem below proves that it always exists and is unique, and the same holds for division with reciprocals.

It follows that $(a + b) - b = a$ and, for $b \ne 0$, $(a \times b) \div b = a$: the second operation undoes the first. Halving undoes doubling in the same way.

blocks.title: Opposite and reciprocal
blocks.body: The opposite $-a$ of a number $a$, also called its additive inverse, is the number with $a + (-a) = 0$: adding it returns to the identity 0. Every number has an opposite (this is what negative numbers supply): the opposite of 5 is $-5$ and the opposite of $-8$ is 8. The reciprocal $\frac{1}{a}$ of a nonzero number $a$, also called its multiplicative inverse, is the number with $a \times \frac{1}{a} = 1$: multiplying by it returns to the identity 1. Every nonzero number has one; the reciprocal of $0.9$ is $\frac{10}{9}$. The number 0 has no reciprocal, since $0 \times x = 0 \ne 1$ for every $x$.

blocks.title: Subtracting is adding the opposite
blocks.body:
For all numbers $a$ and $b$, and $b \ne 0$ in the second,

$$a - b = a + (-b), \qquad a \div b = a \times \tfrac{1}{b}.$$

Note. Since subtraction and division are not associative, an unbracketed chain is read from left to right: $10 - 4 - 2 = (10 - 4) - 2 = 4$ and $16 \div 4 \div 2 = 2$. Written as $10 + (-4) + (-2)$, the chain is a sum, so its terms may be reordered as long as each sign stays with its number: $10 - 4 - 2 = 10 - 2 - 4$. Likewise $16 \div 4 \div 2 = 16 \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{2}$ may be worked in any order.

By the definition of difference we must show that exactly one number added to $b$ gives $a$, and that it is $a + (-b)$. It works:

$$(a + (-b)) + b = a + ((-b) + b) = a + 0 = a,$$

by associativity, then $(-b) + b = b + (-b) = 0$ by commutativity and the definition of the opposite, then the identity. It is the only one: if $x + b = a$, then

$$x = x + 0 = x + (b + (-b)) = (x + b) + (-b) = a + (-b).$$

The laws used are associativity and commutativity of addition, the identity 0 and the existence of the opposite $-b$. The division case is the same calculation with $\times$, $\frac{1}{b}$ and 1 in place of $+$, $-b$ and 0.
Simplify $\frac{7}{15} \times \frac{8}{23} \times \frac{15}{7}$ and $-84n + 73 + 84n$.
blocks.solution:
Bring each number next to its inverse. $\frac{7}{15}$ and $\frac{15}{7}$ are reciprocals, so the product is $\left(\frac{7}{15} \times \frac{15}{7}\right) \times \frac{8}{23} = 1 \times \frac{8}{23} = \frac{8}{23}$.

$-84n$ and $84n$ are opposites, so the sum is $(-84n + 84n) + 73 = 0 + 73 = 73$. In both, commutativity and associativity bring the inverse pair together, the inverse property cancels it, and the identity disappears.

items.q: Why can multiplying by 0 not be undone?
items.a: $3 \times 0 = 0$ and $7 \times 0 = 0$: the result 0 does not record the starting number, so no operation can recover it. This is the same fact as 0 having no reciprocal.
Left to right: $(20 - 5) - 3 = 12$ and $(20 \div 2) \times 5 = 50$. Grouping the other way would give $20 - 2 = 18$ and $20 \div 10 = 2$, both wrong.

items.hint: Rewrite each as a multiplication or an addition using the definitions.

items.q: Show that a number has only one opposite: if $a + x = 0$ and $a + y = 0$, then $x = y$.
items.hint: Work out $(x + a) + y$ in two ways.
items.solution: $y = 0 + y = (x + a) + y = x + (a + y) = x + 0 = x$. The steps use the identity, $x + a = a + x = 0$ (commutativity), associativity, the second equation and the identity again.

items.q: Prove that $-(-a) = a$ for every number $a$.
items.hint: $-(-a)$ is the number which added to $-a$ gives 0. Check that $a$ has this property, then use the previous item.
items.solution: $(-a) + a = a + (-a) = 0$ by commutativity and the definition of the opposite, so $a$ is an opposite of $-a$. By the previous item $-a$ has only one opposite, and $-(-a)$ is one, so $-(-a) = a$. For example, the opposite of $-8$ is 8.

rows.text: American textbooks speak of the commutative, associative, identity and inverse properties. British books more often say laws, or use the nouns: the commutative law or commutativity, the associative law or associativity.
$a \times b$, $a \cdot b$ (a raised dot, common in American algebra books) and $ab$ all mean the same product.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
One more law links the two operations: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ ([[distributive-property]]). With it, the laws of this page are enough to derive all of school arithmetic, including the rules for signs such as $(-1)(-1) = 1$.

Taken as axioms, these properties define the basic structures of algebra. A group ([[groups]]) is a set with one associative operation that has an identity and in which every element has an inverse; the proofs above that the identity and the opposite are unique are, word for word, the first theorems of group theory. The integers under addition form a group, and so do the nonzero fractions under multiplication. A ring ([[rings]]) has an addition and a multiplication linked by the distributive law; the integers, the polynomials and the residues modulo $n$ ([[congruences]]) are rings.

Commutativity is the law most often lost. Matrix multiplication ([[matrices]]) is associative but not commutative:

$$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix},$$

while the product in the other order is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Even associativity fails for numbers stored by a computer, which rounds after every step: in standard double-precision arithmetic $(0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3$ comes out as $0.6000000000000001$ but $0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3)$ as $0.6$.

- Addition and multiplication are commutative, $a + b = b + a$, and associative, $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$; so sums and products of any length may be reordered and regrouped freely.
- Subtraction and division are neither; chains are worked left to right, or rewritten as sums of opposites and products of reciprocals, which may then be reordered.
- 0 is the identity for addition and 1 for multiplication; an identity is always unique. $a \times 0 = 0$, and division by 0 is undefined.
- $c - b$ is the number which added to $b$ gives $c$, and $c \div b$ the number which multiplied by $b$ gives $c$; so subtraction and division undo addition and multiplication.
